articles.title: This Biglaw Co-Founder’s Side Project Was Engineering A Revolution
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

In the early 1900s, a founding partner of which Wall Street law firm was hired by French investors desperate to recoup their losses on a failed canal project and ran one of the most audacious lobbying campaigns in American history, steering the U.S. government to route its canal through Panama instead of Nicaragua, helping to bankroll and orchestrate a revolution that split Panama off from Colombia, and collecting an $800,000 fee for his trouble?

Hint: Part of the campaign involved mailing U.S. senators Nicaraguan postage stamps depicting an erupting volcano, to scare them off that route for the canal.

See the answer on the next page.

articles.title: James Ho Demands First Amendment Right To Post Covert Bathroom Pics
articles.content:
A couple weeks ago, Judge James Ho used a concurrence to complain that it’s unfair that people accuse judges of auditioning for promotions. Late last week, he wrote a dissent as part of his audition for a promotion.
On Friday, the Fifth Circuit voted 10-7 against an en banc rehearing of Evans v. Garza. This case involved a woman seeking to block a potential prosecution against her for — checks notes — posting a surreptitious picture of someone in a bathroom. Because, you know, the First Amendment should protect bathroom candids!
In May 2023, Michelle Evans, a Texas GOP activist, went to a Texas House debate about gender-affirming care for minors. In the Capitol’s women’s restroom, she encountered a trans woman who was running for the Texas House at the time. After confronting the candidate outside the restroom, Evans went back to the gallery, where a seatmate showed her a Facebook photo that someone from their group had taken of the candidate washing her hands at the sink. Evans then posted it to Twitter, racking up some 1.6 million views.
The Texas Penal Code § 21.15(b) made it a state jail felony to photograph or transmit “a visual image of another in a bathroom or changing room” without consent and “with intent to invade the privacy of the other person.” The local prosecutor opened an investigation based on the fact that Evans… did that. Evans, backed by Elon Musk’s X, sued to block any prosecution on First Amendment grounds.
This seems like a pretty good law to have! Judge Priscilla Richman, concurring in the denial, explained why the statute makes this an easy case:
The Texas Legislature reached the considered judgment that everyone, be it the Governor, a member of the Texas House or Senate, a state or federal judge, a political activist, a tourist, or a child, should have protection from being photographed without their consent when in a restroom, when the intent is to invade their privacy. This is a substantial, legitimate state interest.
Evans challenged the law on its face, which Richman describes as a non-starter because “it is highly unlikely that there is a First Amendment right to distribute, without their consent, images of a person’s genitalia (whether they be an adult, infant, pre-teen, or teen) while utilizing bathroom facilities.” As for an as-applied challenge, Evans argued that, despite the broad language of the statute, it shouldn’t apply once a person left the stall and stands at the sink.
Adult lawyers argued that maybe some parts of the bathroom should be fair game for photographs. Richman asked “as to urinals, does the First Amendment say cameras can click once the pants or trousers are zipped?” before opting not to rewrite the statute on this one.
But Judge Ho saw an opportunity. In dissent, Ho frames the facts as an attempt to stifle conservative speech, as though we make laws against creepers installing cameras in bathrooms to oppress conservatives:
After all, the photo depicts the individual in question in precisely the same way that that person chooses to present himself in public. So if that’s a violation of privacy, then we have truly lost all understanding of the word.
A creeper snapping pictures of a teen girl in the bathroom would also show her in the way she presents herself in public, but that doesn’t make it okay. Ho leads off his dissent lamenting that the law should apply equally to everyone, though he declines to grapple with the logical conclusion of opening the door to start snapping away inside bathrooms. Meanwhile, Richman actually put in the effort to explain what it would mean to apply Ho’s standard evenly.
Presumably — or at least hopefully — Ho doesn’t actually believe that this law should be struck down to open the door to every pedophile on free speech grounds. But it’s a convenient hook for him to draft a Townhall blog post masquerading as a judicial opinion and that’s what it takes to stay atop the potential Supreme Court promotion power rankings.
One of Ho’s principal rivals in those power rankings, Judge Andy Oldham, wrote his own dissent. “Travis County District Attorney Garza wanted to prosecute Michelle Evans over a tweet,” he writes, before citing a story about Pakistani human rights lawyers sentenced to 17 years for social media posts. I’m not sure the human rights lawyers put in jail for calling out their government for running a terrorist state presents an apples-to-apples comparison to taking stealthy bathroom pics, but Oldham swings for the fences.
If Ho’s opinion reads as a blog post, Oldham reached for a book report of The Trial:
Kafka’s Inspector said, “I can’t even confirm that you are charged with an offense, or rather I don’t know whether you are. You are under arrest certainly, more than that I do not know.” . . . That was not supposed to be an instruction manual.
Ooh, Kafka. How literary! While Kafka’s protagonist was placed under arrest and tried for an unknown charge, Evans was… none of those things. The local prosecutor investigated the case, but Evans was never arrested or charged or put on trial. She sought an injunction against potential prosecution herself and, at the end of the day, this case died because the prosecutor told the court that the office isn’t moving forward with anything anyway.
So Oldham’s opinion adopts the same flawed frame as Ho’s:
Never mind that the tweet constituted political speech. And never mind that criminally charging social-media users for core political speech is tragicomically unconstitutional in this country.
The problem was never political speech, the problem was YOU CAN’T POST PICTURES OF PEOPLE IN BATHROOMS. It doesn’t become legal to traffic in bathroom pics just because someone slaps a political excuse on it.
Oldham likes to posture as “the reasonable one” in the SCOTUS race compared to fellow hopefuls like Ho and the Ninth Circuit’s VanDyke, but he’s really the same except he wants you to know he’s the kind of guy who read his senior year English assignments.
Anyway, back to Ho. Because here’s the most bizarre part of his audition:
I’m well aware that today’s decision captures the cultural zeitgeist of societal elites. Just a few months ago, the Supreme Court used a female pronoun to describe the male plaintiff in the caption of its decision in West Virginia v. B.P.J.
Does this case have anything to do with the B.P.J. case other than tangentially involving a trans person? No. Indeed, the Supreme Court sided with the conservatives in that case. This case isn’t even really about trans rights, it’s about whether there’s a First Amendment exception to posting bathroom pictures if the plaintiff asserts a First Amendment interest in pictures of people taking a piss. But Ho’s clearly been hankering to go on a tirade about the Supreme Court accepting the caption rather than taking the symbolic act of unilaterally changing it. The conservative legal movement is just style over substance all the way down.
This reads like Ho had this cooked up for a caption that actually involved a pronoun dispute, but then the Alito retirement chatter convinced him that perfect could not be the enemy of the good and he decided this was a good enough hook to hang this on. All so he could send the message that most of the conservatives on the Supreme Court are liberal squishes, but that Ho would be willing to stand up to the scourge of living with a caption.
So I’m grateful to have this opportunity to dissent. I only regret that we could not extend that same privilege to Michelle Evans.
Evans dissented to 1.6 million people — Richman even adds that, aside from everything else, Evans could’ve conveyed the exact same message without the picture — and the only repercussion she faced was temporarily handing over her phone.
When Ho complained that there’s no way for a judge to refute the charge that he’s auditioning, he overlooked one option. Stop sending in tapes.
(Full opinion on the next page…)

articles.title: ‘Adventures In Legal Tech’: Where Knowledge Management Meets AI
articles.content:
Law firms are pouring money into AI adoption right now, hoping a new tool will magically organize decades of scattered knowledge.
Nobody threw anything away, but almost nobody organized it either, notes Rachel Shields Williams, the director of AI and knowledge management at Bass, Berry & Sims and president of the Legal Marketing Association.
In this episode of “Adventures in Legal Tech,” Rachel joins host Jared Correia to discuss the state of most firms’ data and how the industry can manage it more effectively.
AI Can Do Everything, Right?
Wrong. The real work, Rachel says, happens before any AI tool touches your files.
Respecting the ‘Riptide’
Using technology in a law firm can also be a lot like swimming in the ocean. Here, Rachel explains why.
The Full Conversation
Curious to learn more? Check out this episode below
The post ‘Adventures In Legal Tech’: Where Knowledge Management Meets AI appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: AI And Front-End Loading: The Highest And Best Use
articles.content:
I spent a good part of my professional life trying lawsuits. So when I saw the recent AI Guide for Litigators from the Thomson Reuters Institute (TRI) and ILTA, I paid attention. I’ve generally found TRI’s work to be insightful. It is typically free of thinly disguised sales pitches found in much of the supposedly substantive content offered by vendors.
TRI’s Guide rightly notes that AI tools can be used at virtually any stage of litigation. But the description of AI use in early case assessment (which TRI calls ECA) and outcome analysis (both of which I’ve always heard described as front-end loading) stood out for me. It could indeed be AI’s highest and best use in litigation.
TRI’s Guide
Here’s how TRI describes what AI can do at this early stage:
· Analyze large volumes of materials to assess a matter’s scope, facts, and likelihood of success.
· Pre-litigation case assessment, comparing the current matter against historical precedents.
· Identify key custodians and timelines.
· Inventory and characterize matters of fact or law potentially relevant to the case.
· Highlight patterns, gaps, inconsistencies, or other anomalies in evidence.
· Identify advantageous arguments, venues, and courts.
Why did this stand out? Because in my view, this initial stage of any case is the most important one to get right. But it is often the one that clients balk at paying for.
ECA. It’s Critical
Why do I say it is the most important? Because if you get this correct, it provides you with the vision and strategy for the rest of the case. It helps you formulate your themes. It will expose your case’s strengths and weaknesses. From the beginning.
I learned over the years that knowing this can help you determine how the case should best end. Is it a case to be settled? When? And, most importantly, at what number? Or is it one that has to be tried? If done right, it will reveal what your client really hopes to achieve. The true objective.
ECA will determine your relationship with other defendants, if any. It enables you to direct the client where the case will be going and what to expect. It will form the basis of determining who and what type of expert witnesses you will need. It will help you identify who you need to depose. It will determine your motion practice and the timing of motions. It will guide you in determining the relevant documents and enable you to master those documents.
I had some pretty good mentors along the way. One used to say the first thing he would do when a case came in the door was to draft the jury instructions. Another would spend a couple of hours looking out the window thinking before he did anything. Both used these techniques to guide their underlying approach for the rest of the case.
What these mentors were trying to do was in fact the very early case assessment and outcome analysis that the Litigation Guide discusses. They were front-end loading.
Those Pesky Clients
But pre-AI, front-end loading took time. A lot of time. And that was the rub. Often, clients would tell me they did not want to pay for the time needed to do the kind of analysis that I thought needed to be done at the outset of the case.
Why? Several reasons, all related to cost. Some clients were in denial, thinking maybe the case would go away, so why pay for the work. Or that the plaintiff’s lawyer would not put in the time to pursue it or pursue it well. Or was not capable. Some believed that the exposure did not justify the time needed to do a good early analysis. Some figured the work could just be done later if it proved necessary or it could be spread out. The “one step at a time” approach.
The High Cost Of Back-End Loading
All of which was wrong, of course. Later always adds costs. And not doing a robust early case analysis and trying to catch up with back-end loading inevitably leads to more time and cost. Not doing it often digs you into a hole that is expensive and difficult to get out of.
I took over a case once because the existing lawyer did not do this kind of early analysis. He allowed his first witness to be deposed early in the case without doing the work needed. His intuition was that his case was pretty strong, and he thought he would save the client costs. (Or maybe he was just lazy.)
His intuition held up right until the time the plaintiff’s lawyer slid a document across the table. A document the defense lawyer hadn’t found. A document he hadn’t vetted with the client and its witness. A document that looked deadly and for which the witness could offer no explanation. I can only imagine how the faces of the witness and the lawyer dropped when that one showed up.
Now the case had a serious problem. We recovered, but it took a lot of work and rehabilitation later on. Overall costs skyrocketed. Never saw that previous lawyer again, by the way. Early work is critical.
Enter AI, Stage Right
So what does this have to do with the TRI Guide and AI? It’s simple. AI can substantially reduce the cost and time of doing this front-end work. It can do things like help create an initial chronology, identify key legal issues, match claims to evidence, identify critical witnesses, develop a litigation plan, assess expert witness needs and identification, evaluate motions that could be filed, analyze damages, and identify key documents. Good and bad. What do we know? What do we not know?
And perhaps most important for the clients, it can help develop a litigation budget. A budget based on an actual strategy instead of somebody pulling numbers out of thin air and hoping the client doesn’t ask too many questions.
Not only can this kind of assessment be made at a fraction of what it used to cost, but it can also save costs throughout the litigation. Identify key issues and witnesses early and maybe you conclude you don’t need 25 depositions. You instead need fewer and more pointed depositions and more pointed discovery. Or you decide not to waste time and money filing certain motions.
The cost savings will run throughout the litigation and enable this kind of assessment to be made in almost any case, big or small. It’s quite an advantage.
And The Human?
From this AI work, the trial lawyer can determine what really matters and what the exposure of the case really is from day one, not on the eve of trial. Which guides every other decision. So front-end loading is the most important thing you will do in litigation. And you now have a tool that will do most of the work at a fraction of the time and cost.
That leaves the lawyer to do what they do best. Looking out the window and applying their judgment and experience to all the front-end grunt work.
And that’s the real highest and best use AI can have. In any litigation.
Stephen Embry is a lawyer, speaker, blogger, and writer. He publishes TechLaw Crossroads, a blog devoted to the examination of the tension between technology, the law, and the practice of law.
The post AI And Front-End Loading: The Highest And Best Use appeared first on Above the Law.

The cost savings will run throughout the litigation and enable this kind of assessment to be made in almost any case, big or small. It’s quite an advantage.

And The Human?

From this AI work, the trial lawyer can determine what really matters and what the exposure of the case really is from day one, not on the eve of trial. Which guides every other decision. So front-end loading is the most important thing you will do in litigation. And you now have a tool that will do most of the work at a fraction of the time and cost. 

That leaves the lawyer to do what they do best. Looking out the window and applying their judgment and experience to all the front-end grunt work.

And that’s the real highest and best use AI can have. In any litigation.
